World Winter Time Zones

Every country and region is coloured by the clock it keeps in winter, without daylight saving. Places with the same colour share the same clock. Hover or tap a zone to see who lives in it.

Time zones in winter

    Faint lines mark every 15° of longitude, which is one hour of sun time. Small circles mark island groups too small to draw at this scale. Click a zone or a chip to keep it highlighted. Swipe the map sideways to see all of it.

    How this was worked out

    Which clock counts as winter

    • Each place is shown on the clock it keeps in its own winter. North of the equator that is the December to February clock. For Australia, New Zealand and Chile it is the June to August clock, so in January those places run one hour ahead of what the map shows.
    • Some zones only line up in winter: Arizona joins the rest of US Mountain time at UTC−7, and Manitoba and Saskatchewan share UTC−6.
    • British Columbia stays on UTC−7 this winter after adopting permanent daylight time, so Vancouver now shares a colour with Calgary and Phoenix.
    • Morocco and Western Sahara moved to permanent UTC+0 on 20 September 2026.
    • China uses UTC+8 nationwide, so Xinjiang is drawn on UTC+8 rather than its informal local time. Crimea is drawn on UTC+3, as the tz database records it, while Ukraine’s population figure is counted at UTC+2.
    • Offsets come from the IANA tz database (2026e); boundaries from the timezone-boundary-builder release of the same version. Antarctica is left off.

    Where the population numbers come from

    • Country totals are World Bank estimates for 2025. Taiwan uses its household register (June 2026). Western Sahara is an approximate 0.6 M.
    • Countries that span several zones are split by state or province: US Census 2025 estimates, Rosstat 2025, IBGE 2022 census (Brazil), INEGI 2020 census (Mexico), Indonesia’s 2020 census, Statistics Canada 2021 census, ABS March 2026 (Australia) and 2019 provincial estimates for DR Congo.
    • States split between zones (the Florida panhandle, western Kentucky, East Tennessee, El Paso and others) and outlying islands (Canaries, Azores, Bougainville, Galápagos and others) use rounded figures, so treat the smallest zones as approximate.
    • The zone totals add up to the World Bank’s world figure. Tiny territories with no World Bank estimate (each under 20,000 people) are left out.
